note: Draft general guidance compiled from university extension fact sheets (sources below). Not a substitute for a local agronomist or extension officer. No chemical products or doses are given on purpose: follow local labels and expert advice.
general: Work with plants only when the leaves are dry; wet plants spread bacteria and spores.
Clean hands, knives and tools between plants and after handling diseased ones.
Remove affected material from the field: do not compost it or leave it between rows.

none: No action needed. Keep checking plants every few days, especially after rain or cool, damp weather.
Keep irrigation at the base of plants and early in the day so leaves and heads dry quickly.

black_rot.why: Bacterial disease (Xanthomonas campestris) spread by water splash, tools and seed; favoured by warm, wet weather.
early: Pick off the affected leaves (yellow V-shaped patches from the leaf edge) when the plant is dry, and bag them.
Check neighbouring plants: black rot spreads along the row with splashing water.
Switch overhead watering to drip or base watering if possible.
moderate: Remove all affected leaves; remove the whole plant if the veins inside the stem are black.
Stop working in the block while it is wet and clean tools after touching these plants.
Ask a local extension officer whether a protective spray is advisable (sprays only slow spread; they do not cure).
severe: Remove and destroy badly affected plants to protect the rest of the crop.
Plan at least 2 years without cabbage-family crops in this spot and control cruciferous weeds.
Next season: use certified disease-free seed or transplants and resistant varieties.
critical: The plant is unlikely to recover: pull it out and destroy it away from the field.
Treat the area as infected: 2-3 year rotation away from cabbage-family crops and clear all crop residue.
black_rot.check: Check before acting: black rot starts at the leaf EDGE as yellow V-shaped areas pointing inward along a vein, and the veins inside them turn black. It does not grow grey or purple fuzz under the leaf. If you see angular yellow patches between the veins with grey-white fuzz underneath instead, it is more likely downy mildew.

downy_mildew.why: Fungus-like pathogen (Hyaloperonospora) favoured by cool (10-15 C), humid weather and long leaf wetness.
early: Remove the spotted leaves and improve airflow: thin crowded plants and clear weeds around them.
Water in the morning at the base of the plant so leaves are dry by evening.
Watch closely during cool, damp spells: this is when it spreads fastest.
moderate: Remove affected leaves and keep the canopy open; avoid overhead irrigation completely.
Ask a local extension officer about a protective treatment while cool, wet weather continues (treatments protect new growth, they do not cure infected leaves).
severe: Remove heavily infected leaves or plants; check whether the head (curd) shows grey-brown discolouration.
Harvest healthy heads early if the weather stays cool and wet.
critical: Remove and destroy the plant; clear all residue at the end of the season.
Next season: 2-3 year rotation away from cabbage-family crops, disease-free transplants, wider spacing.
downy_mildew.check: Check before acting: downy mildew gives angular yellow-to-brown patches bounded by the veins, with grey-white or purplish fuzz on the UNDERSIDE (easiest to see on humid mornings). If the yellow areas start at the leaf edge as V-shapes with blackened veins inside, it is more likely black rot, which is bacterial and handled differently. This model can confuse the two on leaves with yellow V-shaped edges.

bacterial_spot_rot.why: Bacterial rot of the head (curd) that enters through wounds and water sitting on the head; favoured by wet, mild weather.
early: Keep the head dry: stop overhead watering during head development and water early in the day.
Avoid damaging heads and leaves during weeding or harvest; wounds let bacteria in.
If the head is near maturity, harvest soon and cut away the affected area.
moderate: Harvest affected heads now if usable; cut well beyond the discoloured area with a clean knife.
Clean the knife between heads and do not store affected heads with healthy ones.
Improve airflow around the remaining plants and keep water off the heads.
severe: The head is unlikely to be marketable: remove it and destroy it away from the field.
Check nearby heads daily; rot can spread quickly in wet weather.
critical: Remove the whole plant and destroy it (do not compost).
Clear crop debris after harvest and use clean, well-drained water sources for irrigation.
bacterial_spot_rot.check: Check before acting: bacterial rot of the head is SOFT, wet or slimy, often smells bad, and the brown tissue collapses when pressed. Downy mildew on the head instead gives dry grey-brown discoloration of the curd surface, usually with downy mildew patches (grey-white fuzz underneath) on the leaves of the same plant. This model can confuse the two on heads.

insect_damage.why: Holes and chewed leaf edges are made by leaf-eating insects (caterpillars such as diamondback moth, cabbage looper and cabbage white butterfly; also flea beetles) or by slugs and snails. It is not a disease.
insect_damage.check: Turn leaves over and look at the growing point: green caterpillars, eggs or droppings point to caterpillars; many tiny round holes and small jumping beetles to flea beetles; slime trails to slugs or snails.
early: Look on the undersides of leaves and in the growing point for caterpillars and eggs; pick them off and destroy them.
Check again in 3-4 days: a few holes on older outer leaves rarely affect the head.
Spare natural enemies (parasitic wasps, ground beetles, spiders): avoid broad-spectrum sprays.
moderate: Check about 25 plants spread across the field (undersides of lower leaves) to see how widespread the pests are.
Ask a local extension officer about the action threshold and suitable, preferably selective or biological, control before spraying; always follow the product label.
Protect young plants with fine insect netting where practical, and keep cabbage-family weeds down around the field.
severe: Damage is heavy: act soon, especially if the young head or the growing point is being eaten.
Get advice from a local extension officer on control suited to the pest you found; follow local labels.
After harvest remove crop residues, and avoid planting cabbage-family crops in the same field in consecutive years.
critical: The leaves are mostly eaten: protect the remaining plants first and get local expert advice quickly.
Heavily eaten young plants may not recover; consider replacing them.
After harvest remove crop residues, and avoid planting cabbage-family crops in the same field in consecutive years.
